Christopher Carthy.bio: Christopher Carthy is the Chairman of the Town of North Castle Planning Board, a role he has held for many years (documented in board minutes and resolutions from at least 2017 through 2025). Professionally, he is the principal and founder of Pools of Perfection, an Armonk-based swimming-pool design, construction and service company (523 Main Street, Armonk, NY), where he has roughly three decades of experience designing and building pools. He is deeply embedded in local civic life: he serves as a Vice President of the Armonk Chamber of Commerce, as a Director of the Friends of the North Castle Public Library (helping set up the Armonk Outdoor Art Show), and has sat on the Town of North Castle Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee in addition to chairing the Planning Board. His background is that of a local business owner and hands-on builder rather than an attorney or engineer, which shows in his practical, site-oriented approach to land-use review.

keyIssues: Wetlands and buffers, and coordination with the Conservation Board on mitigation plans
Parking, traffic and site access arrangements
Tree removal, landscaping and visual screening of new development
Zoning and land-use conformance, including subdivision plat amendments
Neighbor concerns and site-specific safety/impact considerations
Practical, well-documented site design informed by actual field/topographic conditions
engagement.likes: Carthy responds well to applicants who do visibly high-quality, well-prepared work and who engage collaboratively through iterative revisions, repeatedly praising strong plans as 'much better,' 'tremendous improvement,' or 'amazing' work. He values site walks and firsthand observation of conditions (he discloses his own informal site visits and welcomes Conservation Board site walks), and he rewards proposals that formalize landscape and wetland-mitigation commitments and demonstrate substantial conformance with prior approvals.
engagement.dislikes: He is more guarded on neighbor-impact and safety themes (his lowest-sentiment area), so proposals that appear to disregard adjacent-property or community concerns draw his skepticism. He also expects wetland/buffer and screening issues to be addressed with formal, Conservation-Board-satisfying plans rather than vague assurances, and he scrutinizes parking, traffic and access changes to confirm they are truly the only or de-minimis changes claimed.
engagement.recommendation: Come to Carthy with a clean, professional, well-illustrated package and be explicit about what has changed since the last submission, characterizing minor revisions honestly as de minimis / in substantial conformance where accurate. Proactively formalize landscape, screening and wetland-mitigation plans and show they have been coordinated with the Conservation Board, and invite or reference a site walk so decisions rest on real topographic and field conditions. Pre-empt neighbor and safety concerns directly, and frame revisions as a collaborative improvement over prior iterations; his supportive instinct is strong when applicants demonstrably engage in good faith and do careful work.

Christopher Carthy.notes: Identity is confidently established via a clear North Castle/Armonk nexus: the same Christopher Carthy is Planning Board Chairman and principal of the Armonk firm Pools of Perfection, with corroborating civic roles (Armonk Chamber of Commerce, Friends of the North Castle Public Library, Comprehensive Plan Steering Committee). Name-collision caution: a separate 'Chris Carthy, President of Armentum Partners' on LinkedIn is a DIFFERENT person and not the North Castle official. Email left blank rather than guessed. Engagement analysis is grounded primarily in first-party observed meeting behavior (avg sentiment +0.27 across 98 positions; most positive on wetlands/buffers, most cautious on neighbor concerns & safety) plus representative supportive quotes.

Steven Sauro.bio: Steven ('Steve') Sauro is a long-serving member of the Town of North Castle (Armonk, NY) Planning Board, where he has sat for roughly a decade; town meeting minutes show him active since at least 2017, when he served for a period as Acting Chairman, and he continues to serve as a member alongside Chairman Christopher Carthy. In meetings he presents as technically fluent on site-engineering matters (stormwater systems, infiltration/Cultec detail, siting and grading) and frequently carries applications to a vote, indicating a senior, trusted role on the board. His profession and employer could not be confirmed from the public record, and North Castle does not publish individual board-member email addresses, so identifying details beyond his civic role are limited.

keyIssues: Stormwater and drainage engineering (infiltration systems, metering runoff vs. existing conditions)
Wetlands and buffer protection
Steep slopes and rock/blasting removal
Tree removal and vegetative screening
Parking, traffic and site access
Practical, workable regulation (e.g., pushing the Town Board to allow Level 3 EV charging where siting made it sensible)
engagement.likes: He responds well to technically rigorous applications that show, with specifics, that a project performs as well as or better than existing/neighboring conditions (his Cultec/stormwater argument at 1613 Old Orchard Street is the archetype). Well-sited, 'straightforward' proposals that have already absorbed site-walk feedback, and pragmatic solutions that answer a real concern, earn his support and often his motion to approve.
engagement.dislikes: His engagement is coolest on steep-slope/rock-removal and tree-removal/screening themes, where his sentiment runs lowest, so aggressive grading, blasting, or loss of mature screening tends to draw his scrutiny. He is skeptical of arguments that ignore practical, on-the-ground realities of a site.
engagement.recommendation: Bring him the engineering, not just the concept: quantified stormwater/drainage performance versus existing conditions, clear grading and rock-removal limits, and a credible tree-preservation and screening plan will do more than aesthetics. Demonstrate that you have walked the site and addressed prior board feedback, and frame requests in terms of practical, workable outcomes. Pre-empt his likely concerns on slope disturbance and tree loss up front; if you win his technical confidence he is frequently the member who moves approval.

Steven Sauro.notes: Identity as the North Castle Planning Board member is high confidence: name recurs across town Planning Board minutes from 2017 (as Acting Chairman) through recent years alongside Chairman Christopher Carthy, matching the assigned role. No individual municipal email was found: the town website (northcastleny.com / .gov) returned 403 on direct fetch and North Castle routes Planning Board contact through the Planning Department (17 Bedford Road, Armonk; 914-273-3000 ext. 43) rather than publishing per-member addresses; email left blank per instructions rather than guessed. Engagement analysis is grounded in first-party meeting-behavior data (avg sentiment 0.23; 40 positions).

Michael Pollack.bio: Michael Pollack is a member of the Town of North Castle Planning Board and a veteran real estate attorney with more than 30 years of experience. He is a partner at the New York real estate law firm Adler & Stachenfeld LLP (which he joined in 2022), where he practices in the firm's Corporate Real Estate and Leasing groups and co-chairs its Construction practice; his work centers on the purchase, sale, and financing of major commercial properties, lease and ground-lease transactions, construction contracts, and development. He earned his J.D. from Boston University School of Law and is admitted to practice in New York. Beyond the Planning Board, he represents North Castle in county land-use matters, serving as Vice Chairman of the Westchester County Airport Advisory Board and Co-Chair of the Westchester County Inter-Municipal Airport Master Plan Task Force. His professional grounding in commercial real estate, leasing, and land development directly informs the technical, code-focused lens he brings to Planning Board review.

keyIssues: Strict compliance with the town code and zoning process (variances, expirations, permit sequencing)
Parking adequacy, traffic and site access
Neighbor concerns and public safety on the site
Steep slopes, rock removal and site engineering
Bonding, maintenance and enforceable conditions of approval (e.g., insurance)
Design quality and neighborhood/homeowner fit
engagement.likes: He responds well to applications that are procedurally clean, well-documented, and demonstrably code-compliant, and he rewards patience and thorough technical work (he praised the 'impressive' Phase 1B at 76 Virginia Road and read survey conclusions into the record). He is supportive of attractive, context-sensitive designs and is willing to let homeowners make reasonable choices about their own property, offering constructive mitigation ideas such as landscaping to soften wall height. He appreciates collaborative, site-walk-driven outcomes.
engagement.dislikes: He is skeptical of anything that shortcuts the zoning process or the town code: at 12 Maple Avenue he read Section 355-77 aloud, argued an expired ZBA variance meant 'without a variance you don't have a site plan,' and said extending the resolution was 'against the town code.' Large deviations from standards draw his opposition, as when he flagged a roughly 400% parking reduction as 'a problem for me.' He wants risks closed off through enforceable conditions rather than assurances.
engagement.recommendation: Come to Pollack with the legal and procedural groundwork already airtight: confirm variances are current and permits are properly sequenced, and cite the specific town-code sections you are relying on before he does. Bring hard technical documentation (surveys, engineering, parking counts, slope/rock analyses) and justify any deviation from a standard with data rather than narrative. Frame requests as enforceable conditions of approval he can point to, and proactively offer maintenance, bonding, or insurance commitments. Respect the process he values, acknowledge neighbor and safety concerns directly, and emphasize design quality and neighborhood fit to earn his support.

Michael Pollack.notes: Identity confirmed via strong town nexus: named on the North Castle Planning Board page/staff directory and cited by name in North Castle Planning Board minutes (2017, 2020) and Examiner coverage of the Armonk Summit Club approval; professional identity corroborated by the Adler & Stachenfeld attorney bio and LinkedIn. No personal municipal email was found — the town website (northcastleny.com) returned HTTP 403 to direct fetches, and North Castle Planning Board members generally are not assigned individual town email addresses; Planning Board correspondence typically routes through the Planning Department (Town Hall, 17 Bedford Road, Armonk, NY 10504). Email left blank rather than invented per spec. Minor name-collision risk: several unrelated 'Michael Pollack' individuals exist (e.g., Marcus & Pollack property-tax attorneys, an NYU Schack real-estate figure, other attorneys); the Adler & Stachenfeld real-estate partner is the one consistently tied to North Castle and Westchester Airport roles. Bio confidence high; engagement analysis grounded primarily in first-party meeting behavior from briefs.json.

Thomas Crispi.bio: Thomas Crispi (often addressed as 'Tom' in meetings) is a volunteer member of the Town of North Castle Planning Board (Armonk, NY), one of five residents appointed by the Town Board to review site plans, subdivisions, wetlands permits and special-use referrals. His profession, employer, education and length of tenure could not be independently confirmed in the public record accessible for this dossier; the town's official Planning Board roster and staff directory (northcastleny.com) could not be retrieved, and web searches surfaced several unrelated same-named individuals rather than a verified profile of the North Castle official. Based on his observed conduct he functions as an engaged, detail-oriented board member who is comfortable with technical/engineering discussion (grading, drainage, tunnel and water-infrastructure specifics) and routinely makes and seconds approval motions. Beyond his Planning Board service, no other civic roles or community ties are confirmed here.

keyIssues: Parking, traffic circulation and site access (his most positively-engaged theme)
Wetlands, buffers and environmental mitigation
Steep slopes, rock removal and retaining-wall engineering on constrained lots
Zoning and land-use conformity
Construction execution, contractor logistics and public safety during work (e.g., motorist protection/egress)
Fair treatment of current applicants versus legacy/pre-existing site disturbances
engagement.likes: He responds well to pragmatic, workable proposals backed by clear technical answers, and treats common site-design constraints (like tight gas-station or lot circulation) as facts to be managed rather than reasons to block a project. He is receptive to applicants who distinguish their current proposal from prior owners' actions, and is visibly impressed by well-explained, high-benefit infrastructure and engineering work.
engagement.dislikes: His skepticism is mild rather than adversarial, surfacing as more measured, lower-sentiment engagement on environmentally sensitive elements: wetlands and buffers, retaining walls, and steep-slope/rock-removal work, where he wants sound technical justification. He presses for specifics on how work will actually be executed and on safety impacts before he is comfortable moving forward.
engagement.recommendation: Come prepared with concrete engineering detail and address site circulation, access and parking head-on, since that is where he engages most constructively. Pre-empt his environmental and site-stability concerns by bringing wetland/buffer, steep-slope, rock-removal and retaining-wall specifics, plus a clear construction-logistics and public-safety plan (contractors, sequencing, motorist/egress protection). Where a site carries legacy disturbances, clearly separate your application from prior owners' conduct. He is a generally supportive, solutions-oriented vote once the technical case is credible, so respect the board's process and give him substance to second a motion on.

Lawrence Ruisi.bio: Lawrence J. Ruisi ("Larry"), a longtime Armonk resident (North Castle, zip 10504), is a retired media/entertainment executive and career corporate director who serves as a volunteer member of the North Castle Planning Board. A Certified Public Accountant, he earned a B.S. in accounting and an MBA in finance from St. John's University and began his career at Price Waterhouse & Co. before rising to Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer of Columbia Pictures Entertainment and then President & CEO of Loews Cineplex Entertainment Corporation, the movie-theatre operator he helped form from the 1998 Sony/Loews-Cineplex Odeon merger. As a non-executive he has served on numerous public-company boards, frequently as audit-committee chair and designated financial expert, including Athene Holding (director since 2013, audit-committee chair), Hughes Communications, UST Inc., InnKeepers USA Trust, Wyndham International and Adaptec, and he has taught as an adjunct accounting professor at St. John's University. His finance/CFO background is evident in his detailed, technical approach to Planning Board matters.

keyIssues: Neighbor safety and off-site impacts (errant golf balls, hazards crossing property lines)
Parking, traffic and access adequacy (pushing realistic, code-based capacity figures)
Tree removal, buffers and screening between lots
Stormwater and drainage management
Fire-code and technical compliance / defensible occupancy numbers
Clean process and procedure, and coordination with other agencies (e.g., Town Board, highway dept.)
engagement.likes: He responds well to applications that answer his technical questions clearly and are grounded in defensible, code-based numbers rather than optimistic estimates — e.g., he preferred the ~17-space fire-code capacity figure as "more realistic and defensible" and called a Level 3 EV charger proposal something that "makes all the sense in the world." He is reassured by concrete, verifiable mitigation such as plantings and tree buffers near sensitive features (septic, property lines), and by common-sense fixes; he explicitly agreed that pulling golf tees closer would "substantially reduce" his concern. He also values local, on-the-ground knowledge and interagency coordination.
engagement.dislikes: His skepticism spikes on neighbor-safety and off-site risk: he warned he would "certainly vote no" on a use that could send golf balls into a neighbor's yard, unwilling to accept the risk of someone "getting smacked in the head." He is wary of capacity or impact figures he sees as understated or not defensible, and dislikes proposals that leave residual hazards to adjacent properties unaddressed. His near-neutral sentiment on process/procedure suggests low tolerance for sloppy or incomplete submissions.
engagement.recommendation: Come prepared for a CFO-style, numbers-first review: bring code-referenced calculations (parking, fire-code occupancy, stormwater) and be ready to defend every figure as realistic, not aspirational — he will test them and rewards the more conservative, defensible number. Proactively map and mitigate any off-site or neighbor impact (safety hazards, sightlines, drainage, tree/screening buffers along property lines) before the hearing, since unresolved neighbor risk is his firmest 'no.' Answer his technical questions directly and completely; when he is satisfied he will move a project forward (he has made the motion to approve). Acknowledge local conditions he may know firsthand and show coordination with the Town Board, highway department, and other agencies.
